title: Input Validation with Bean Validation
description: Add validation constraints to your DTOs and entities using Jakarta Bean Validation.

slides.title: Why Validate? 🛡️
slides.content:
# Never Trust Client Input

Your API should always validate incoming data before processing it. Bean Validation (JSR‑380) allows you to declare constraints on fields using annotations like `@NotNull`, `@Size`, `@Email`, and many more.

When validation fails, Spring throws a `MethodArgumentNotValidException`, which you can handle globally.

quizData.question: Which annotation is used to enable validation on a controller method parameter?
quizData.explanation: Use `@Valid` (from jakarta.validation) to trigger validation on an object.

slides.title: Using @Valid in Controller
Common Validation Annotations 📋
slides.content:
# Built‑in Constraints

| Annotation | Purpose |
|------------|---------|
| `@NotNull` | Value cannot be null |
| `@NotEmpty` | CharSequence/Collection/Map not null and not empty |
| `@NotBlank` | String not null and not empty after trimming |
| `@Size(min, max)` | Size of string, collection, array |
| `@Min(value)` | Numeric value >= value |
| `@Max(value)` | Numeric value <= value |
| `@Email` | Valid email address |
| `@Pattern(regexp)` | String matches regex |
| `@Past` / `@Future` | Date in the past/future |

You can also create custom constraints.

slides.title: Validation Groups 🔧
slides.content: You can group constraints (e.g., for create vs update) using validation groups. We'll cover that in advanced topics.
